ratings.plot: In Mumbai, Nurse Prabha's routine is troubled when she receives an unexpected gift from her estranged husband. Her younger roommate, Anu, tries in vain to find a spot in the city to be intimate with her boyfriend.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Kapadia's debut is a precise, patient film about two women in Mumbai finding small moments of freedom, shot with rare visual clarity on 35mm.

ratings.plot: In the twilight of Francisco Franco's dictatorship, an 8-year-old orphan and her two sisters find shelter in the house of their stern aunt and try their best to acclimatize to a new reality. Can they summon up the courage to grow up?

verdict.reason: Essential Saura on 35mm at a theater built for this work. A masterpiece about childhood resilience under Franco's shadow that demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: Impersonal and beautiful images of Akerman's life in New York are combined with letters from her loving but manipulative mother, read by Akerman herself.

verdict.reason: A landmark film about maternal distance and New York life—essential Akerman on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the spare, precise images sing.

ratings.plot: A thorough and unvarnished analysis of Elon Musk, a technology billionaire who serves as the CEO of Tesla, SpaceX, and Twitter.

verdict.reason: Alex Gibney brings his investigative rigor to a figure who shapes the present moment. A documentary this thorough demands a big screen while the subject remains in motion.

ratings.plot: Rural New Zealand, 2006. Over one transformative summer, 14 year-old Sid Bookman discovers desire, identity and the internet, as she imitates the people she longs to be loved by.

verdict.reason: A debut about teenage self-invention in the pre-smartphone era deserves a big screen. Schneideman captures the specific texture of 2006 desire and digital yearning with precision.

movies.title: ONCE UPON A TIME IN HARLEM

ratings.plot: A decade post-death, filmmaker William Greaves reveals his final work: footage of a 1972 gathering he arranged with Harlem Renaissance legends, which he deemed his most significant capture.

verdict.reason: A lost Greaves documentary surfaces with pristine restoration at Lincoln Center. Rare archival footage of Harlem Renaissance figures in 1972 makes this essential cinema history.

ratings.plot: Thirty-four days before she's sent to prison, notorious Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait becomes a mind-bending three-year journey.

verdict.reason: Nathan Fielding and Lance Oppenheim have made something genuinely disorienting about power, performance, and the camera's complicity—a three-hour document that earns its runtime. The film's structural ambition (letting Holmes control her own image while the filmmakers undermine it) is best experienced on the big screen where the manipulation becomes tactile.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in the Middle East

ratings.plot: Xu Fu worked as head chef of a Chinese restaurant in Middle East, running the Dragon Restaurant with manager Ma Junsheng.

verdict.reason: A rare film about ordinary life amid conflict deserves the big screen. Muye Wen's debut captures a restaurant's resilience through a chef and manager's partnership in wartime.

ratings.plot: Four strangers' paths cross by chance, leading to complex emotional entanglements that challenge their existing relationships and force them to confront uncomfortable truths about love and commitment.

verdict.reason: Lee Chang-dong's first film in a decade demands the big screen and your full attention. Nearly three hours of moral complexity and emotional precision—see it before word spreads.

ratings.plot: Follows filmmaker Eleanor Coppola's behind-the-scenes documentation of her daughter Sofia Coppola directing the 2006 film MARIE ANTOINETTE, capturing the craftsmanship and challenges of being a young female director.

verdict.reason: Eleanor Coppola's behind-the-scenes doc captures Sofia directing her breakthrough film—rare access to a major artist at work. Ninety minutes of pure filmmaking craft, no filler.

ratings.plot: In secret conversations on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza are revealed by the people who designed and operated them.

verdict.reason: Essential testimony from the people who built Israel's targeting systems, shot in the dark on Tel Aviv rooftops. The 80-minute runtime keeps the weight intact without padding.

ratings.plot: The foundations of Grayson Manor are shaken when an accident leaves Boyd Grayson handless and his mother invests in radical new technology to help him.

verdict.reason: Glenn McQuaid's perfect-scored horror film about body horror and maternal obsession demands a theater. The restored print at Alamo Drafthouse is the only way to see it tonight.

ratings.plot: A daughter unravels her father's dark past after his body, missing for 36 years, is found at a horrific crime scene.

verdict.reason: A debut feature hitting 100% is rare enough to trust. Downey's direction turns a missing-body mystery into something genuinely unsettling.

ratings.plot: Cameron Winter, in December 2025, after a months-long sold-out tour with his band Geese, returned to New York to play a single show at Carnegie Hall. This is the movie. Directed and shot on 35mm and 16mm by Oscar-winning filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson (ONE BATTLE AFTER ANOTHER), the crew includes filmmaker and actor Benny Safdie (THE SMASHING MACHINE) and music producer Ariel Rechtshaid (Grammy winner for albums with Vampire Weekend and Adele). GQ praised Cameron Winter’s show at Carnegie Hall as “staggeringly good,” and Nick Cave said he has "a glorious, emotive voice with brilliant, blistering words, a racked and wondrous thing.” Winter’s solo album Heavy Metal was named one of the best of the year by Pitchfork , Rolling Stone , Paste , and Mojo , and Geese’s last record Getting Killed was named the best album of 2025 by The New Yorker , NME , and Stereogum .

verdict.reason: Paul Thomas Anderson shot a 72-minute concert film on 35mm and 16mm for a performer whose album dominated year-end lists. See it theatrical before it vanishes.

ratings.plot: An enduring, singular masterpiece of cinema starring Academy Award®-winner Vanessa Redgrave and Oliver Reed, KEN RUSSELL’S THE DEVILS is a prescient epic of obsession and corruption, and a defining work of art from seminal filmmaker Ken Russell. Assembled from the original camera negative, this new 4K restoration presents Ken Russell’s definitive vision of THE DEVILS by referencing the edit he privately constructed in 2004. KEN RUSSELL’S THE DEVILS is the uncut and unfiltered theatrical experience that Russell always envisioned – and the first time, the film will be presented restored and in 4K.

verdict.reason: Russell's unfiltered masterpiece demands the big screen in this definitive 4K restoration. The 2004 edit he privately constructed finally gets theatrical release as intended.

ratings.plot: A bored photographer recovering from a broken leg passes the time by watching his neighbors and begins to suspect one of them of murder.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's perfect thrillers—see it on a big screen where every window frame matters. Hitchcock's control of suspense through pure visual storytelling has no equal.

ratings.plot: A high-strung news producer finds herself in a love triangle between a talented but self-doubting reporter and a charming new anchor, who embodies the growing trivialization of news that she is determined to fight against.

verdict.reason: One of the sharpest films about journalism, ambition, and the cost of principle — see it restored at Metrograph while it plays. Holly Hunter's performance is a masterclass in conveying intelligence and heartbreak through restraint.

ratings.plot: A psychopath tries to forcibly persuade a tennis star to agree to his theory that two strangers can get away with murder by submitting to his plan to kill the other's most-hated person.

verdict.reason: Hitchcock's masterpiece of psychological manipulation deserves the big screen. The 35mm print at Metrograph shows why the geometry of his shot-making still cuts.

ratings.plot: Portrait of a middle-class family in Taipei. A man in his forties, his teenage daughter and his eight-year-old son experience life, navigating between remorse, hope and disappointment.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for Edward Yang's three-hour masterpiece on family life and time's passage. Metrograph's DCP restoration honors the precision of Yang's composition and color.

ratings.plot: A young woman suspects her neighbors have sinister plans for her pregnancy.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's great paranoia films—see it on 35mm at Metrograph. Polanski's control of suspense and Mia Farrow's performance define the modern horror picture.

ratings.plot: A filmmaker applies lessons from a Hallmark movie writing workshop to pitch a documentary about concrete.

verdict.reason: John Wilson's deadpan conceptual comedy deserves the big screen. A Hallmark workshop applied to concrete is the kind of absurdist premise only he executes this well.

ratings.plot: The story of Danish soldier and explorer Ludvig Kahlen, who explored and cultivated Denmark's wild Jutland, which now comprises the vast majority of the country, in the mid-18th century.

verdict.reason: Arcel's 127-minute epic earns a trip to Film Forum. The scale and ambition of this historical drama justify the theatrical commitment.

ratings.plot: Direct continuation of Takashi Yamazaki's Godzilla Minus One.

verdict.reason: Takashi Yamazaki returns to finish what he started—essential for anyone who saw Minus One. A 119-minute continuation from the director of that film demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: Fifteen years after murdering his sister on Halloween night 1963, Michael Myers escapes from a mental hospital and returns to the small town of Haddonfield, Illinois, to kill again.

verdict.reason: Carpenter's lean, methodical filmmaking defined the slasher template and still works as pure cinema. Ninety-one minutes of sustained dread—every frame counts, no fat.

ratings.plot: A research chemist comes under personal and professional attack when he decides to appear in a 60 Minutes exposé on Big Tobacco.

verdict.reason: Mann's corporate thriller holds up as essential political cinema. Metrograph is screening it on 35mm, the format that captures his obsessive cinematography.

ratings.plot: Self-doubt, sacrifice and struggle converge into an existential crisis for a devoted classical vocalist as the mastery he strives for remains elusive.

verdict.reason: A rare New York screening of Tamhane's austere masterpiece about classical music and spiritual doubt. The 129-minute runtime and chamber intimacy demand the theater's focus.

movies.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

ratings.plot: Follows Latif, a devoutly religious hitman, who embarks on a desperate journey across Houston to protect his children after his wife dies, confronting forces closing in and beliefs threatening to unravel.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for Tariq's urgent action filmmaking and a hitman role that strips away genre cliché. Catch it in 35mm while it's in theaters.

ratings.plot: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

verdict.reason: Nolan on 70mm is always worth the trip, and a nearly three-hour epic demands the biggest screen in the room. Catch it at Lincoln Square or Sheepshead Bay in IMAX before it leaves.

ratings.plot: After enduring years of malfunctioning products, Wile E. Coyote teams up with a local personal injury attorney to take on ACME, the manufacturer of anything and everything used by the Looney Tunes characters.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for a Looney Tunes film that actually lands the joke. Dave Green finds real comedy in the lawsuit premise instead of coasting on nostalgia.

ratings.plot: Follows a hapless courier tasked with delivering a package to a remote hospital. He soon finds himself caught in the middle of an outbreak and must fight through hordes of mutated creatures to survive.

verdict.reason: Zach Cregger makes action horror that actually lands—this one's worth seeing on IMAX. A 90-minute creature-feature shoot-out with real craft behind the mayhem.

ratings.plot: A young man murders women, using a movie camera to film their dying expressions of terror.

verdict.reason: Powell's masterpiece belongs on the big screen in this restoration. The camera itself becomes the weapon—a formal and moral choice that still cuts deep.

ratings.plot: During her family's move to the suburbs, a sullen 10-year-old girl wanders into a world ruled by gods, witches and spirits, and where humans are changed into beasts.

verdict.reason: One of the greatest animated films ever made deserves the big screen. Miyazaki's hand-drawn world is hypnotic and demands theatrical scale.

ratings.plot: "The Washington Post" reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein uncover the details of the Watergate scandal that leads to President Richard Nixon's resignation.

verdict.reason: Essential political thriller that defined the genre and still moves like a freight train. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the craftsmanship in every frame.

ratings.plot: In 19th century Massachusetts, the March sisters--Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy--on the threshold of womanhood, go through many ups and downs in life and endeavor to make important decisions about their futures.

verdict.reason: Gerwig's take on this story justifies the trip, especially on Metrograph's screen. The 135-minute runtime and formal precision reward theatrical attention.

ratings.plot: In an increasingly Westernized postwar Tokyo, an aging widower arranges a marriage for his only daughter.

verdict.reason: Ozu's final film is essential—a masterwork of stillness and domestic grace at a major venue. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the precise geometry of every frame.

ratings.plot: Meeting a stranger in a railway station, a woman is tempted to cheat on her husband.

verdict.reason: One of the great films about desire and restraint—see Lean's precision on 35mm at Metrograph. The restored print makes every glance and hesitation cut like glass.

ratings.plot: When a nobleman is threatened by a family curse on his newly inherited estate, detective Sherlock Holmes is hired to investigate.

verdict.reason: Terence Fisher's 1959 take is the definitive Sherlock adaptation on screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this the night to catch it.

movies.title: If I Go Will They Miss Me

ratings.plot: A boy sees ghostly figures of other boys in his neighborhood while grappling with his father's distance. These visions uncover hidden connections between them and their shared heritage.

verdict.reason: A bold debut that fuses supernatural vision with intimate family drama. Thompson-Hernandez's visual language justifies the theatrical bet.

ratings.plot: In 1944 Francoist Spain, an imaginative young girl meets a faun who tells her she's a princess and that she must prove her worthiness by completing three dangerous tasks.

verdict.reason: Del Toro's masterwork demands the big screen and dark theater it deserves. The creature design and visual invention reward theatrical immersion in ways streaming cannot match.

ratings.plot: The untold and inspiring tale of one of the most important mountain climbers in history who, with Edmund Hillary, became the first person to reach the summit of Mount Everest.

verdict.reason: A major biographical film about mountaineering history from the director of Sherpa. Peedom brings visual mastery to Everest's untold story.

movies.title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown

ratings.plot: A television actress encounters a variety of eccentric characters after embarking on a journey to discover why her lover abruptly left her.

verdict.reason: Essential Almodóvar on 35mm at Metrograph. The 1988 restoration glows on film; this is how the color and rhythm were meant to land.

movies.title: The Flavor of Green Tea Over Rice

ratings.plot: A childless middle-aged couple faces a marital crisis.

verdict.reason: Essential Ozu on 35mm at Metrograph. A masterwork about marriage and compromise that demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: While on a trip to Paris with his fiancée's family, a nostalgic screenwriter finds himself mysteriously going back to the 1920s every day at midnight.

verdict.reason: Allen's best work in years—a romantic fantasy that earns its charm without straining. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the cinematography to what it should be.

movies.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma

ratings.plot: A director making a slasher sequel becomes obsessed with casting the original film's 'final girl,' leading both women into psychological and sexual chaos.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun's collision of horror, sex, and meta-filmmaking deserves a big screen. The psychological tangle between director and actor plays best in a theater.

ratings.plot: After breaking the mysterious "One Wish Willow" to win his crush's heart, a hopeless romantic finds himself getting exactly what he asked for but soon discovers that some desires come at a dark, sinister price.

verdict.reason: Curry Barker's high-concept horror delivers real scares with a premise that actually pays off. The 4DX format amplifies the body horror and dread at Times Square or Sheepshead Bay.

ratings.plot: An unfinished creation leaves his isolated castle and enters a suburban world eager to embrace him ~ until his differences become impossible to ignore. What begins as a modern fairy tale gradually becomes a story about loneliness,...

verdict.reason: Burton's most tender film deserves revival on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings new life to the autumnal palette.

ratings.plot: Explores what it means to be gay throughout different eras, focusing on "three existences" that are connected through themes of sexuality, desire, pain, and inheritance.

verdict.reason: Ambitious 155-minute musical-drama from the Javiers hits hard on desire and inheritance. The 35mm print at Angelika is a rare theatrical event.

ratings.plot: A high-school boy in the early 1970s is given the chance to write a story for Rolling Stone magazine about an up-and-coming rock band as he accompanies them on their concert tour.

verdict.reason: Crowe's best film about the messy collision of fandom, fame, and growing up deserves the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the 1970s rock aesthetic sing.

ratings.plot: An upper-class widow falls in love with a much younger, down-to-earth nurseryman, much to the disapproval of her children and criticism of her country club peers.

verdict.reason: Sirk's melodrama remains essential—class collision, forbidden desire, and visual depth that only 35mm can deliver. Metrograph's 35mm print is the only way to see this film tonight.

ratings.plot: An immigrant Romanian family living in Norway is subject to an investigation and faces the scrutiny of the local judicial system.

verdict.reason: Mungiu's methodical thriller about scrutiny and suspicion grips you in silence. His measured pacing demands full attention in a dark room.

ratings.plot: When a young boy's family is killed by the mob, their tough neighbor Gloria becomes his reluctant guardian. In possession of a book that the gangsters want, the pair go on the run in New York.

verdict.reason: Cassavetes' kinetic crime thriller demands the big screen and a crowd. Gena Rowlands improvises circles around the mob plot with a performance that defines the film.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in China

ratings.plot: Legendary martial arts hero Wong Fei-Hung fights against foreign forces' plundering of China. When Aunt Yee arrives back from America, Wong Fei-Hung assumes the role of her protector.

verdict.reason: Essential action cinema from Hark Tsui at peak invention. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the wire work and editing snap with clarity.

ratings.plot: A cyborg assassin from the future attempts to find and kill a young woman who is destined to give birth to a warrior that will lead a resistance to save humankind from extinction.

verdict.reason: Essential action cinema—see it on the big screen at Metrograph. Cameron's control of pace and image design still dominates the room.

ratings.plot: A teenager at Rushmore Academy falls for a much older teacher and befriends a middle-aged industrialist. Later, he finds out that his love interest and his friend are having an affair, which prompts him to begin a vendetta.

verdict.reason: Anderson's deadpan comedy about adolescent obsession holds up perfectly on the big screen. Metrograph is showing the DCP restored, which sharpens every witty frame and musical cue.

ratings.plot: A troubled marine seeks to reconcile with the survivors of an Iraqi family he and his unit fired on back in 2003.

verdict.reason: A serious reckoning with American military violence that earns its runtime. Reed Van Dyk directs with the kind of moral weight that demands a theater seat, not a smaller screen.

ratings.plot: Two death-obsessed sisters, outcasts in their suburban neighborhood, must deal with the tragic consequences when one of them is bitten by a deadly werewolf.

verdict.reason: Smart werewolf film where the monster is a metaphor for female rage and transformation. It earns its genre credibility and cult status.

ratings.plot: A sheltered and manipulative Southern belle and a roguish profiteer face off in a turbulent romance as the society around them crumbles with the end of slavery and is rebuilt during the Civil War and Reconstruction periods.

verdict.reason: Essential cinema history on the big screen, even at four hours. Fleming's direction, the Technicolor, and the sheer scale of the production demand theatrical immersion.

ratings.plot: The chief of a police unit that can accurately predict and prevent crimes goes on the run after he's accused of a future murder himself.

verdict.reason: Spielberg's 2002 thriller holds up as sharp sci-fi action with real ideas about power and guilt. Metrograph's DCP presentation makes the futuristic New York pop on the big screen.

ratings.plot: After his mother's sudden death, Socrates, a 15-year-old living on the margins of São Paulo's coast, must survive on his own while coming to terms with his grief.

verdict.reason: A precise, unsentimental film about a teenager adrift after loss in São Paulo's margins. At 71 minutes, Moratto's direction cuts straight to the bone without wasting a frame.

ratings.plot: When Jonathan Harker rouses the ire of Count Dracula for accepting a job at the vampire's castle under false pretenses, his friend Dr. Van Helsing pursues the predatory villain.

verdict.reason: Fisher's 1958 vampire classic demands the big screen—the saturated Technicolor and sharp 35mm print at Metrograph make this essential. Lean 82 minutes of pure gothic atmosphere.

ratings.plot: In 2004, an ad director faces a turbulent Christmas weekend. In 2026, a filmmaker turns her story into a screenplay, blurring the lines between reality, fiction, and the people closest to him.

verdict.reason: Almodóvar playing with reality and fiction across two decades deserves a big screen. The layering of autobiography and invention is exactly what this director does best.

ratings.plot: Isolated from the rest of the world in their countryside mansion, an unhappily married couple engages in a series of increasingly violent role playing games in an effort to heal their relationship.

verdict.reason: Saura's 1969 film belongs in a theater, especially this restoration at Metrograph. The escalating games between the couple demand the intensity of a big screen.

ratings.plot: When the attempt to kill a professor goes wrong, a series of violent events are triggered which force a taxi driver to run for his life.

verdict.reason: Na Hong-jin's kinetic action thriller demands a theater. The DCP restoration at Metrograph makes this the right time to catch two hours of relentless pursuit and collision.

ratings.plot: A woman narrates the contemplative writings of a seasoned world traveler, focusing on contemporary Japan.

verdict.reason: Marker's masterpiece of philosophical travel and montage demands the big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph brings decades of accumulated texture into sharp focus.

ratings.plot: Harry's dead and, while no one really minds, everyone feels responsible. After Harry's body is found in the woods, several locals must determine not only how and why he was killed but what to do with the body.

verdict.reason: Hitchcock's rare comedy-mystery hybrid deserves the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this 1955 gem sparkle with sharp dialogue and visual wit.

ratings.plot: A young girl risks everything to prevent a powerful, multinational company from kidnapping her best friend - a fascinating beast named Okja.

verdict.reason: Bong Joon Ho's genre-bending adventure earns a big-screen trip. Metrograph's DCP presentation honors the creature design and scale that streaming can't match.

ratings.plot: In 1950s Connecticut, a flustered housewife faces a marital crisis and mounting racial tensions in the outside world.

verdict.reason: Todd Haynes' 1950s melodrama is essential cinema on the big screen. Metrograph's 35mm print restores the saturated color and formal precision that define the film.

ratings.plot: Medea is in Corinth with Jason and their two young sons. King Kreon wants to reward Jason for his exploits: he gives the hand of his daughter, Glauce, to Jason as well as the promise of the throne. In exchange, Medea and the boys ...

verdict.reason: Von Trier's stark vision of ancient tragedy demands the big screen and Metrograph's print. Seventy-six minutes of ruthless formal control over raw emotion.

ratings.plot: The story of charismatic painter Wladyslaw Strzeminski, who opposed social realism and maintained his own artistic freedom in spite of political obstacles.

verdict.reason: Wajda's final film about artistic defiance against totalitarianism deserves the big screen. Film Forum's restoration honors a master's last statement on creative freedom.

ratings.plot: In 2006, To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen sets out to make television history.

verdict.reason: Lance Oppenheim made a sharp film about a TV moment that defined the 2000s. The subject—Hansen's obsession with televised justice—gives the director real material to work with.

ratings.plot: In 1977, disability rights activist Judy Heumann leads a historic 28-day occupation of San Francisco's Federal Building, uniting protesters in a fight for accessibility laws and equal rights.

verdict.reason: Sian Heder directs a historical turning point that demands the big screen. The 504 Sit-In is cinema—practical urgency, moral clarity, and human stakes that hit harder in a theater.

ratings.plot: An Okinawan prophecy appears to foretell Earth's destruction at the hands of Godzilla, only for the true Godzilla to reveal his doppelganger as a mechanical alien weapon.

verdict.reason: A lean 84-minute Godzilla film with a genuinely clever premise—the monster you think is the villain is actually the hero. Jun Fukuda keeps the pace moving and the twist lands.

ratings.plot: After being institutionalized in a mental hospital, Su-mi reunites with her sister, Su-yeon, and they return to live at their country home. But strange events plague the house, leading to surprising revelations and a shocking conc...

verdict.reason: Kim Jee-woon's debut is a visual and psychological masterpiece that rewards big-screen immersion. The twist recontextualizes everything before it, making repeat viewings essential.

ratings.plot: A devoted wife is visited by her mother, a successful concert pianist who had little time for her when she was young.

verdict.reason: Bergman's late masterpiece about mothers and daughters cuts deeper than any therapy session. Metrograph's restoration makes the chamber drama breathe on the big screen.

ratings.plot: While awaiting execution for murder, Baron Victor Frankenstein tells the story of a creature he built and brought to life - only for it to behave not as he intended.

verdict.reason: Terence Fisher's 1957 horror is essential Hammer—see it restored on the big screen. The DCP at Metrograph brings out the color and craft that made this film matter.

ratings.plot: While passing through a vacation resort, a newlywed couple encounters a mysterious, strikingly beautiful countess and her aide.

verdict.reason: A rare 1971 vampire film with genuine visual style and erotic menace. Kümel's compositions and the countess's performance justify the theatrical experience.

ratings.plot: Five friends head out to rural Texas to visit the grave of a grandfather. On the way they stumble across what appears to be a deserted house, only to discover something sinister within. Something armed with a chainsaw.

verdict.reason: Essential horror cinema that demands the big screen. Tobe Hooper's lean 83 minutes generates more dread than most films twice as long.

ratings.plot: The unenviable life of a government-agency clerk takes a horrific turn with the arrival of a new co-worker who is both his exact physical double and his opposite otherwise--he's a confident, charismatic ladies' man.

verdict.reason: Ayoade's visual control and Jesse Eisenberg's dual performance justify the trip. Metrograph's DCP presentation sharpens the film's crisp, deliberate framing.

ratings.plot: The spirits of a deceased couple are harassed by an unbearable family that has moved into their home, and hire a malicious spirit to drive them out.

verdict.reason: Burton's comic horror is best on the big screen. Metrograph is showing the 35mm print.

ratings.plot: Two best friends fall in love with a pair of women, but the relationships soon go in very different directions.

verdict.reason: Ken Russell's 1970 adaptation brims with visual audacity and erotic intensity that demands the big screen. The wrestling scene alone justifies the trip to IFC.

ratings.plot: After being kidnapped and imprisoned for fifteen years, Oh Dae-Su is released, only to find that he must track down his captor in five days.

verdict.reason: Park Chan-wook's revenge masterpiece demands the big screen. Metrograph's DCP presentation locks in the angular compositions and color that make this film sing.

ratings.plot: A rain-soaked couple take refuge in the castle of a transvestite mad scientist from outer space who is about to unveil his greatest creation.

verdict.reason: A cult classic that demands the midnight-movie theater experience with a live crowd. Jim Sharman's 1975 musical is built for audience participation and collective absurdity.

ratings.plot: Vampire hunter Dr. Van Helsing returns to Transylvania to destroy handsome bloodsucker Baron Meinster, who has designs on a beautiful young schoolteacher.

verdict.reason: A sharp Hammer vampire film in pristine 35mm at Metrograph. Terence Fisher's baroque direction and lurid Technicolor make this essential on the big screen.

ratings.plot: One of the most successful designers in high fashion plans his fall 1994 collection. Follow the behind-the-scenes look at the creative side of fashion.

verdict.reason: A sharp doc about fashion's creative machinery from a rare 35mm print at Film Forum. Keeve's behind-the-scenes access captures design obsession in real time.

ratings.plot: Macbeth, the Thane of Glamis, receives a prophecy from a trio of witches that one day he will become King of Scotland. Consumed by ambition and spurred to action by his wife, Macbeth murders his king and takes the throne for himself.

verdict.reason: Kurzel transforms Shakespeare into a visceral war film that demands the big screen. The staging and cinematography justify the theatrical trip to Lincoln Center.

ratings.plot: The Candyman, a murderous soul with a hook for a hand, is accidentally summoned to reality by a skeptic grad student researching the monster's myth.

verdict.reason: A genuinely unnerving horror film that earns its scares through mood and mythology. Bernard Rose's direction turns urban legend into something tactile and real.

ratings.plot: A businessman accidentally kills The Metal Fetishist, who gets his revenge by slowly turning the man into a grotesque hybrid of flesh and rusty metal.

verdict.reason: A rare DCP screening of a 67-minute cult landmark at Metrograph. Tsukamoto's body-horror visionary work demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: An anthology of 5 different cab drivers in 5 American and European cities and their remarkable fares on the same eventful night.

verdict.reason: Jarmusch's five-city taxi anthology is a minor classic worth seeing in 35mm. Metrograph's print captures the deadpan humor and nocturnal intimacy that define the film.

ratings.plot: A young college student arrives in a sleepy Massachusetts town to research witchcraft; during her stay at an eerie inn, she discovers a startling secret about the town and its inhabitants.

verdict.reason: A lean 1960s horror film with genuine atmosphere and a twist that lands. The inn setting and small-town dread feel earned, not manufactured.

ratings.plot: A rookie cop spends his first day as a Los Angeles narcotics officer with a rogue detective who isn't what he appears to be.

verdict.reason: Denzel Washington's corrupt detective is magnetic enough to carry a solid crime thriller. The power dynamic between rookie and mentor crackles across 122 minutes.

ratings.plot: A psychosomatically blind, deaf, and mute boy becomes a master pinball player and, subsequently, the figurehead of a cult.

verdict.reason: Ken Russell's opera-rock fever dream demands a big screen and full volume. The pinball sequences and Tina Turner alone justify the subway ride.

ratings.plot: A wealthy New York City investment banking executive, Patrick Bateman, hides his alternate psychopathic ego from his co-workers and friends as he delves deeper into his violent, hedonistic fantasies.

verdict.reason: Harron's satire of '80s Wall Street excess still cuts deeper than most horror films. The image design and Bale's performance make this essential viewing on the big screen.

ratings.plot: Female artists, writers, photographers, designers, and adventurers are settled in Paris between the wars.

verdict.reason: A rare look at the women who built modernism in interwar Paris, restored and screening at Metrograph. Seventy-five minutes is the right length for a documentary that moves.

ratings.plot: Con artists plan to fleece an eccentric family using an accomplice who claims to be their long-lost uncle.

ratings.plot: The allure of stardom on the big screen proves to be a road to some very dark places for Mia Goth’s titular PEARL in this stylish and gruesome prequel to Ti West’s X. With her husband away at war, Pearl finds herself dreaming of a way to escape from her boring life on the farm. She sees the silver screen as her way to find stardom and the love she so desperately needs, but her overbearing mother and her own dark impulses might hold her back from the fame she craves. PEARL proves to be a delightfully perverse study on a standout character from writer/director Ti West’s tribute to ‘70s grindhouse, X. Its vibrant, candy-coated veneer plays wonderfully against the depraved desires of the main character bubbling just below the surface. Co-writer/star Mia Goth gives another deliciously unhinged performance as Pearl, a not-quite-innocent farm girl looking for love in all the wrong places. As much a love letter to the Golden Age of Hollywood as it is a demented look at the darkness bubbling just below the surface of rural America, PEARL is colorful, unnerving, and twisted in all the right ways.

Their oddball host, Chester (Oliver Woolf), feeds them, helps them recover, and introduces a system of rewards: behave yourself, earn “nifties,” cash them in for hot-tub time and dance parties. Beyond the cottage, things are less nifty. But within it, a makeshift family is taking shape. While Liam embraces their new life, Mel grows increasingly curious about the world Chester insists is too dangerous to enter… In their feature debut, directors Scott Tinkham and Michael Woloson mix deadpan comedy, sibling rivalry, and creeping unease in a coming-of-age story about people who have to grow up all over again. Winner of the Special Jury Prize at the 2026 Manchester Film Festival and the Narrative Feature Audience Award at Dances With Films LA 2026, this has the sort of sensibilities that fans of Yorgos Lanthimos and Ben Wheatley will adore… and it’s a natural fit as an Alamo Exclusive.

ratings.plot: Where would we be without PSYCHO? Sixty years on and Hitchcock’s delicious cod-Freudian nightmare about a platinum-blonde embezzler (Janet Leigh) who neglected to consult a guide before selecting her motel still has much to answer for. It blazed a bloody trail for the much-loved slasher cycle, but it also assured us that a B-movie could be A-grade in quality and innovation. It dared to suggest that your star didn’t need to surface from an ordeal smelling of roses (or, indeed, at all). It combined a knife, a scream, a melon, some chocolate sauce, Bernard Herrmann’s greatest score, and more than 70 edits to push the envelope of screen violence. It lent The Simpsons some of its best gags. It offers perfect case studies of suspense, paranoia, and montage for lazy film studies tutors. And, of course, it was the first movie to show a toilet flushing, so we might also credit it with spawning the entire gross-out genre. PSYCHO: We salute you. (David Jenkins, Time Out )

A mysterious discovery is made on the outskirts of the remote harbor town. The residents find themselves in a desperate fight for survival against something they have never encountered before.

verdict.reason: Na Hong-jin's three-hour creature feature has ambition and craft, but the runtime tests patience. See it if you're committed to a grueling survival story in a packed theater.

ratings.plot: Presented in a surreal, gory and entirely visual manner, Begotten tells of the death of religion, the abuse of nature by Man and a nihilistic outlook on what life ultimately is.
A young Polish filmmaker sets out to find out what happened to Mateusz Birkut, a bricklayer who became a propaganda hero in the 1950s but later fell out of favor and disappeared.
Maya, a smart, wry nurse, is swept up in an immersive love, that sets her life on a trajectory she never would have imagined.

verdict.reason: Rachel Morrison's directorial debut has real charm but hasn't found its footing yet. Wait for word-of-mouth unless you're committed to a debut romance on a big screen tonight.

ratings.plot: After his quest to retrieve the fabled Golden Fleece, Jason returns to Greece with powerful sorceress Medea. However, when the king banishes her, it's only human that Medea plots her furious revenge. Can they escape her wrath?

A woman discovers the newly resurrected, partially formed, body of her brother-in-law and lover. She starts killing for him to revitalize his body and escape the demonic beings that are pursuing him after he escaped their underworld.
An unconventional single mother relocates with her two daughters to a small Massachusetts town in 1963, where a number of events and relationships both challenge and strengthen their familial bonds.
Three secretaries turn the tables on their obnoxious boss.
In this remake of the classic western, a feared outlaw must decide what kind of man he'll be when the world demands blood.

verdict.reason: Depends on your appetite for revisiting a classic western formula. Julio Quintana stakes the remake on redemption and moral choice rather than spectacle or novelty.

ratings.plot: A story about the most popular racing event in the galaxy, the Redline, and the various racers who compete in it.

A bullied teenage boy is devastated after the death of his heavy metal idol, Sammi Curr. But as Halloween night approaches, he discovers that he may be the only one who can stop Sammi from making a Satanic comeback from beyond the...

verdict.reason: Skip the commute unless you want '80s horror-metal kitsch on a big screen with a crowd. The Alamo Drafthouse shows it as a Halloween throwback, not a restored print.

ratings.plot: A psychiatrist, familiar with the knife-wielding dream demon Freddy Krueger, helps teens at a mental hospital battle the killer who is invading their dreams.

When Fool breaks into the home of his family's landlords, he discovers that they have mutilated several boys and kept them imprisoned under stairs. As Fool attempts to flee, he meets their daughter, Alice. Can Fool and Alice escape?

verdict.reason: Craven's strangest film works as pulp horror-comedy if you surrender to its fever logic. The Nitehawk midnight slot is the right venue for this particular brand of unhinged.

ratings.plot: After an encounter with a neck-biter, a publishing executive thinks that he's turning into a vampire.

With the help of a smooth talking tomcat, a family of Parisian felines set to inherit a fortune from their owner try to make it back home after a jealous butler kidnaps them and leaves them in the country.

verdict.reason: A minor Disney entry, but worth the trip if you catch the 35mm print at Metrograph. The restoration gives the soft pastels and jazzy design real warmth on the big screen.

ratings.plot: The depiction of the life of Nobel Peace Prize winner and founder of Poland's Solidarity movement, Lech Walesa, as events in the 1970s lead to a peaceful revolution.

verdict.reason: Wajda's final film on Poland's Solidarity founder has real historical weight but uneven execution. Film Forum is the right place to see it if you care about the director's legacy.

ratings.plot: A man who has made a new life for himself and the daughter left on his doorstep 6 years ago finds his family threatened when the birth mother resurfaces.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're in the mood for broad comedy-drama that swings for the heart. Derbez's performance carries the film, but the tonal shifts test your patience over two hours.

ratings.plot: A documentary filmmaker and her fellow Generation X graduates face life after college, looking for work and love in Houston.

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming version and catch Stiller's debut on 35mm at Metrograph instead. The print restores the '90s MTV sheen that shaped a generation's self-image.

ratings.plot: The Shelleys visit Lord Byron and compete to write a horror story.

verdict.reason: Ken Russell's chaotic energy works in bursts, but the 87-minute runtime can't sustain his wildest swings. IFC's screening gives the film its best shot on a proper screen.

ratings.plot: A grieving father enacts his long-awaited revenge against a ruthless gang on Christmas Eve.

verdict.reason: John Woo's action direction carries a revenge thriller that doesn't quite land. The Christmas Eve setting and theatrical release matter more than the uneven execution.

ratings.plot: The retelling of France's iconic but ill-fated queen, Marie Antoinette. From her betrothal and marriage to Louis XVI at 14 to her reign as queen at 19 and to the end of her reign as queen, and ultimately the fall of Versailles.

verdict.reason: Coppola's visual style matters more than historical accuracy here. The 123-minute runtime tests patience, but the costume and production design reward big-screen attention.

ratings.plot: A young girl new to a Catholic school befriends a coven of witches whom the other students either shun or fear. But when a powerful invocation goes wrong, the consequences could endanger their lives.

verdict.reason: Skip the weak theatrical cut; it's uneven fun at best and doesn't hold up as horror. The Alamo screening is social viewing, not a restoration reason to go.

ratings.plot: Years after her Hollywood breakthrough, a talented actress whose career has stalled fights for her second act.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're curious about Rock's directorial debut. A middling comedy-drama about a stalled career that doesn't justify the trek to multiplexes.

ratings.plot: A directionless teenager is rushed to a mental institution after a supposed suicide attempt and befriends a group of troubled women who deeply influence her life.

verdict.reason: The 35mm print at Metrograph is worth the trip if you're drawn to Angelina Jolie's performance. Otherwise, the film is uneven and plays better at home.

ratings.plot: A group of 12-year-olds form a Universal Monsters fan club called Monster Squad and attempt to save their hometown from Count Dracula and his fellow monsters when they show up for real.
A mysterious woman, fashion designer by day and prostitute by night, is hounded by two men: a married father of two children and a sexually repressed preacher.

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming version for Ken Russell's unhinged direction on a theater screen. The 1984 35mm print at IFC Center gives this pulp thriller the visual excess it demands.

ratings.plot: In April 1964, twenty years after the Nazis won World War II, S.S. officer Xavier March uncovers a plot to eliminate the attendees of the Wannsee Conference so that Germany can establish better relations with the United States.

verdict.reason: Skip the rental—this alternate-history thriller has real intrigue but uneven execution. Lincoln Center's screening offers the best chance to make it work on a big screen.

ratings.plot: A classic tale about bitter relationships between a frivolous girl and a soldier is adapted for the post-World War II time.

verdict.reason: Clouzot's post-war adaptation has uneven rewards but deserves a look on the big screen. A restored 1949 print at Lincoln Center is the rare chance to see this film as intended.

ratings.plot: Composer and pianist Franz Liszt (Roger Daltrey) attempts to overcome his hedonistic life-style while repeatedly being drawn back into it by the many women in his life and fellow composer Richard Wagner (Paul Nicholas).

verdict.reason: Ken Russell's camp excess and Roger Daltrey's commitment make this worth a look if you're in the mood. The 103-minute runtime keeps the madness from wearing out its welcome.

ratings.plot: An inventor creates a robot that is seized by an undersea kingdom to guide their monster god in attacking the surface as retaliation for the nuclear tests that have devastated their society.

verdict.reason: Skip the 38% film, but catch it at Alamo Drafthouse if you want cheap monster mayhem with a crowd. The 78-minute runtime means you're not stuck in a theater all night.

ratings.plot: A worldwide epidemic encourages a biotech company to launch an organ-financing program similar in nature to a standard car loan. The repossession clause is a killer, however.

verdict.reason: Skip the trip unless you're committed to midnight-movie camp and organ-repo gore. Darren Lynn Bousman's 2008 cult musical has devoted fans, but the Alamo shows are your only shot.

ratings.plot: Filmed in New York, story of naive young woman from Hong Kong who goes to New York to study. Street-wise cabbie cousin takes care of her in the big city.

Elisa hasn't seen her father Luis in nine years, but she receives a telegram from her sister at a time of crisis in their marriage informing her that her father is sick and decides to travel to Madrid to visit Luis for his birthday.

verdict.reason: Saura's 1977 family drama rewards patient viewers but tests endurance at two hours. A rare Metrograph screening of an underknown work by a major Spanish director.

A musician tries to find his inner peace in a cottage within the woods.

verdict.reason: Wajda's 1970 chamber piece deserves a look, but the introspective pace demands patience. Film Forum's restoration makes this the only way to see it properly.

ratings.plot: Antonia Brico dreams of becoming a conductor, but she isn't taken seriously because she is a woman.
A few years after the events of Man of Marble (1977), a journalist investigates Mateusz Birkut's son Maciek Tomczyk, now an activist leading a shipyard strike.

In what might be termed Russo-Shakespearean noir, a ruthless woman's adulterous affair with a drifter sets in motion a chain-reaction of murder and deception in a remote village in 19th Century Mtsensk.

During the Nazi occupation, Jewish prisoner Jakub Gold is released from jail and works as a gravedigger in the Warsaw ghetto. Although he manages to escape and keeps hiding in private apartments, he tries to get back to the ghetto.

ratings.plot: Richard Wagner's last opera has remained controversial since its first performance for its unique, and, for some, unsavory blending of religious and erotic themes and imagery. Based on one of the medieval epic romances of King Art...

verdict.reason: Syberberg's four-hour operatic vision is uncompromising and visually baroque, but demands absolute commitment and tolerance for his deliberately confrontational staging of Wagner's final work. The theatrical experience is singular, though patience and appetite for avant-garde opera aesthetics are prerequisites.

verdict.reason: Saint-Saëns' opera demands the big screen, but this 1981 video production feels dated. Lincoln Center's archive screening preserves a specific performance, not a definitive one.

ratings.plot: A robot girl designed to prevent loneliness tries to save a heartbroken family of humans.

verdict.reason: Waititi's first straight drama has genuine warmth but runs long for its sentiment. The emotional core depends entirely on whether you buy a robot as a conduit for human connection.

ratings.plot: Jay Gardiner is having a whale of a bad day. While diving off the California coast to recover his late father’s remains, he gets swallowed whole by an 80-foot sperm whale and has one hour of oxygen to escape. Austin Abrams, currently having a major moment after starring in Zach Cregger’s RESIDENT EVIL, leads this adaptation of Daniel Kraus’ bestselling novel. Yes, it’s a movie where a guy gets swallowed by a whale, but it’s also a tense and even moving tale of survival, grief, and family. Dive in on the big screen.
Follows a scuba diver who, while looking for his father's remains, is swallowed by an 80-foot, 60-ton sperm whale and has just one hour to get out before his oxygen runs out.

verdict.reason: The premise is genuinely wild, but a debut feature without reviews is a gamble. Catch it at Sheepshead Bay in 4DX if you want the claustrophobic rush amplified.

ratings.plot: After 20 years spent “chillin’, tokin’, and bonin’”, Ali G is shocked to discover that his long-term girlfriend, Julie, is eight months pregnant. Faced with an extra mouth to feed, he gets off his batty and heads to America to reclaim his former glory… but soon encounters adversaries who will ultimately threaten his and his child’s very existence. Sacha Baron Cohen’s new film, ALI G: WHO IZ I? marks his directorial debut and will be released in theaters on October 23 by Amazon MGM Studios.

verdict.reason: Cohen's directorial debut has charm but struggles with uneven pacing over 89 minutes. The Alamo Drafthouse crowd will make it fun; watch it there or skip the trip.

ratings.plot: On October 20, 1967, Roger Patterson captured 59 seconds of film showing a creature walking through the Northern California woods — footage that became the most analyzed and debated in history. Fifty-nine years later, a reel of 16mm film discovered in a safe changes everything. CAPTURING BIGFOOT reveals the untold story behind the world's greatest mystery, told for the first time by Patterson's own son and the people who were there. This is a story about family legacy, broken friendships, and belief itself.
Rising Hollywood star Matt Hagen descends into a horrifying revenge-filled monster when scientific ambition strips him of his identity and humanity.

Presented in Japanese with English subtitles The world-famous classic Alice in Wonderland receives its first Japanese theatrical animated adaptation! Rise Azumino is a university student who feels lost in her life. One day, guided by an invitation letter left behind by her late grandmother, she enters “Wonderland”. She meets a girl named Alice there and they travel together. The Queen of Hearts, the Mad Hatter, Cheshire Cat…the residents of Wonderland appear before Rise one after another and crazy commotion ensues! What kind of future will Rise choose in this crazy adventure with Alice?

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you want a lightweight anime take on Carroll. The premise trades psychological depth for a generic lost-girl-finds-herself journey.

ratings.plot: 40 YEARS OF FUCKIN' UP is SPINAL TAP, but real. It's a film about the infamous, fairly unfamous, and beloved punk rock band NOFX. This is the unbelievable story about how a group of untalented, drug-addicted teenage punks somehow became the most successful independent band in history – and they did it haphazardly, entirely on their own.

verdict.reason: Skip the trip unless you're deep into NOFX or need a loud, sweaty night out. A 131-minute band doc works better as a home viewing with pause buttons for the jokes.

ratings.plot: Street Fighters Ryu and Ken reunite when Chun-Li recruits them for the World Warrior Tournament. As they face a hidden conspiracy, they must confront each other and their past-or face destruction.

verdict.reason: Skip the Alamo unless you want arcade-bar atmosphere with your action film. The tournament setup and revenge subplot work better at home without the noise.

ratings.plot: A Nobel Prize-winning novelist, a director known for bouncing between indie oddballery and giant studio fare, and one seriously stacked cast come together in a sweet sci-fi story. Based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s bestselling novel, Taika Waititi’s adaptation stars Jenna Ortega as Klara, an Artificial Friend looking for a home. She finds one with Josie (Mia Tharia), a teenager whose complicated relationship with her mother (Amy Adams) is shaped by grief and loss. With Natasha Lyonne, Simon Baker, and Steve Buscemi rounding out the cast, there’s plenty to root for in this futuristic family story.
